title: HNSW in one page
description: Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs are the default ANN index for a reason: they answer queries in sub-millisecond time with high recall on a single machine. The index is a layered graph — sparse long-range links on top, dense local links below — and search descends greedily from the top. Construction inserts each vector by searching for its neighbors; queries do the same walk with a wider beam.
mechanism: Layers assigned by exponential decay (most vectors only on layer 0). Insert: greedy search from the top, connect to M nearest on each layer. Query: beam search with efSearch candidates, return top-k.
algo: Query O(log n) hops typical; construction O(n log n). Parameters M (degree) and efConstruction trade build time for recall.
demo:
import random, math, heapq
random.seed(1)
# HNSW idea: greedy walk on a proximity graph (single layer shown)
N, D = 300, 8
vecs = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(N)]

def dist(a, b):
    return math.sqrt(sum((x - y) ** 2 for x, y in zip(a, b)))

# build: each node links its 8 nearest (the 'navigable small world')
g = {}
for i, v in enumerate(vecs):
    g[i] = heapq.nsmallest(8, ((dist(v, u), j) for j, u in enumerate(vecs) if j != i))
    g[i] = [j for _, j in g[i]]

q = [random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)]
cur, best = 0, dist(vecs[0], q)
for _ in range(40):  # greedy descent
    nxt = min(g[cur], key=lambda j: dist(vecs[j], q))
    if dist(vecs[nxt], q) >= best:
        break
    cur, best = nxt, dist(vecs[nxt], q)
exact = min(range(N), key=lambda j: dist(vecs[j], q))
print('greedy found #%d (dist %.3f); exact is #%d (dist %.3f)' % (cur, best, exact, dist(vecs[exact], q)))
print('log-scale hops, not a scan: the small-world property')

title: IVF (inverted file) index
description: IVF partitions vectors with k-means: each vector joins its nearest centroid's list, and queries visit only the nprobe nearest lists. It is the classic accuracy-speed knob — nprobe=1 is fast and lossy, nprobe=100 approaches exact. IVF shines combined with quantization (IVF-PQ): the lists hold compressed codes, so billion-vector indexes fit in RAM.
mechanism: Train centroids on a sample; assign vectors to lists; query: rank centroids by distance, scan the top nprobe lists. Coarse quantizer quality bounds recall.
algo: Query O(C*d + nprobe*(N/C)*d) vs O(N*d) brute force. Train on ~40xC sample vectors.
demo:
import random, math
random.seed(2)
D, N, C = 8, 3000, 32
vecs = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(N)]
centroids = random.sample(vecs, C)

def dist(a, b):
    return math.sqrt(sum((x - y) ** 2 for x, y in zip(a, b)))

lists = [[] for _ in range(C)]
for i, v in enumerate(vecs):
    lists[min(range(C), key=lambda c: dist(v, centroids[c]))].append(i)

q = [random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)]
truth = set(sorted(range(N), key=lambda i: dist(vecs[i], q))[:10])
for nprobe in (1, 4, 16):
    order = sorted(range(C), key=lambda c: dist(q, centroids[c]))[:nprobe]
    cands = [i for c in order for i in lists[c]]
    got = set(sorted(cands, key=lambda i: dist(vecs[i], q))[:10])
    print('nprobe=%2d scanned=%4d recall@10=%.2f' % (nprobe, len(cands), len(got & truth) / 10))

title: Product quantization (PQ)
description: Product quantization compresses each vector to a few bytes: split the dimensions into sub-vectors, k-means each subspace into 256 centroids, and store one byte per subspace (the centroid id). A 128-dim float vector (512 bytes) becomes 8-16 bytes — 32-64x compression. Queries use asymmetric distance: precompute query-to-centroid tables, then score codes by table lookup. Recall loss is typically 1-5%.
mechanism: Split d dims into m subspaces; train 256 centroids per subspace; encode vector as m bytes. Query: build m x 256 distance tables vs the query; score each code by summing table lookups.
algo: Storage m bytes/vector. Query O(m*256*d/m + N*m) table lookups — no float math per vector.
demo:
import random, math
random.seed(3)
D, M, KS = 8, 4, 16  # 4 subspaces, 16 centroids each (4 bits)
vecs = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(500)]
sub = D // M
# train: random centroids per subspace (k-means in production)
codebooks = [[ [random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(sub)] for _ in range(KS)] for _ in range(M)]

def enc(v):
    code = []
    for m in range(M):
        part = v[m*sub:(m+1)*sub]
        code.append(min(range(KS), key=lambda k: sum((a-b)**2 for a, b in zip(part, codebooks[m][k]))))
    return code

codes = [enc(v) for v in vecs]
q = [random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)]
tables = [[sum((a-b)**2 for a, b in zip(q[m*sub:(m+1)*sub], codebooks[m][k])) for k in range(KS)] for m in range(M)]

def adc(code):
    return sum(tables[m][c] for m, c in enumerate(code))

best = min(range(len(vecs)), key=lambda i: adc(codes[i]))
exact = min(range(len(vecs)), key=lambda i: sum((a-b)**2 for a, b in zip(vecs[i], q)))
print('bytes/vector: %d (vs %d float32) -> %dx compression' % (M, D*4, D*4//M))
print('PQ best #%d vs exact #%d' % (best, exact))

title: Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH)
description: LSH hashes so that similar vectors collide: random projections split by hyperplanes give each vector a bit signature, and near-duplicates share signatures. Queries check the buckets matching the query's signature. It is weaker than HNSW/IVF on recall-per-byte today, but the theory is clean, it handles streaming inserts trivially, and it needs no training.
mechanism: k random hyperplanes -> k-bit signature per vector; L tables with different projections; query checks all L buckets, re-ranks candidates exactly. More tables = higher recall, more memory.
algo: Query O(L * bucket size); no training; recall from the (k, L) tradeoff curve.

title: Distance metrics
description: The metric defines 'near': L2 (Euclidean) for raw geometry, cosine for direction (text embeddings are usually cosine/normalized), dot product for learned relevance, Hamming for binary codes. The index must match the metric — HNSW works for any, PQ tables assume L2-ish decomposability. Normalizing vectors turns cosine into L2, which is why 'normalize then L2' is the standard recipe.
mechanism: Choose per embedding model (check its training objective). Normalize for cosine; store norms separately if magnitude matters. The metric is part of the index config, not a query-time choice.
algo: O(d) per comparison regardless of metric; the choice changes results, not speed.

title: Recall@k measurement
description: Recall@k = (retrieved top-k intersect true top-k) / k, measured against exact brute-force ground truth on a query set. It is the single number ANN papers report, and it must be measured honestly: same queries, same k, exact ground truth, no cherry-picking. The recall-latency curve (vary efSearch/nprobe, plot both) is the real comparison — one recall number without its latency is marketing.
mechanism: Compute exact top-k per query offline; run the index; count intersections. Report the curve over parameter settings, plus p99 latency. Datasets: SIFT1M, GIST1M, Deep1B, BigANN.
algo: O(queries * (exact + approx)) measurement. Ground truth computed once, reused.
demo:
import random, math
random.seed(6)
D, N, Q, K = 8, 2000, 20, 10
vecs = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(N)]
queries = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(Q)]

def dist(a, b):
    return math.sqrt(sum((x-y)**2 for x, y in zip(a, b)))

def approx(q, sample=300):  # toy ANN
    idx = random.sample(range(N), sample)
    return sorted(idx, key=lambda i: dist(vecs[i], q))[:K]

recalls = []
for q in queries:
    truth = set(sorted(range(N), key=lambda i: dist(vecs[i], q))[:K])
    got = set(approx(q))
    recalls.append(len(truth & got) / K)
print('mean recall@%d: %.3f over %d queries' % (K, sum(recalls)/Q, Q))
print('honest eval: exact ground truth, same queries/k, plus the latency curve')

title: nprobe / efSearch tuning
description: ANN parameters are recall-latency knobs: nprobe (IVF lists visited), efSearch (HNSW beam width). Tuning means sweeping the knob, measuring the recall-latency curve, and picking the knee — the point where more latency buys little recall. The knee moves with data distribution, so tune on your vectors, not the paper's. Auto-tuning (bandit over the knob at runtime) adapts to load.
mechanism: Grid search over the knob on a validation query set; plot recall vs p99; pick the knee. Runtime: lower the knob under load (graceful degradation), raise when idle.
algo: O(knob values * eval) offline. Online adaptation is a control loop.
demo:
# sweep the knob, find the knee: where latency stops buying recall
curve = [(1, 0.55, 0.2), (4, 0.82, 0.5), (16, 0.95, 1.8), (64, 0.98, 6.5)]  # (nprobe, recall, ms)
print('nprobe recall  latency')
best, best_gain = None, 0
for i, (n, r, ms) in enumerate(curve):
    if i:
        pn, pr, pms = curve[i-1]
        gain = (r - pr) / (ms - pms)  # recall per extra ms
        mark = ' <- KNEE (diminishing returns after)' if gain < 0.05 and not best else ''
        if gain < 0.05 and not best:
            best = n
        print('%6d %.2f   %5.1fms  gain=%.3f recall/ms%s' % (n, r, ms, gain, mark))
    else:
        print('%6d %.2f   %5.1fms' % (n, r, ms))

title: SIMD distance kernels
description: Distance computation is the inner loop of ANN — billions of L2/dot products — and SIMD kernels make each one 4-16x faster. FAISS's kernels use AVX-512 with masked tails; SimSIMD covers every ISA. The kernel fuses the whole distance (load, subtract, FMA, reduce) to stay in registers. This is unglamorous work that decides real-world QPS more than the index algorithm does.
mechanism: Hand-tuned kernels per ISA (AVX2/AVX-512/NEON/SVE); dispatch at runtime by CPUID; masked tails for odd dimensions. Keep vectors 64-byte aligned.
algo: 16 floats/instruction (AVX-512); memory bandwidth usually binds for large scans.
demo:
import time, random
random.seed(7)
D, N = 128, 20000
vecs = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(N)]
q = [random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)]

def scalar():
    return [sum((a-b)**2 for a, b in zip(v, q)) for v in vecs]

def lane4():  # 4-wide accumulation: the SIMD shape
    out = []
    for v in vecs:
        s = [0.0]*4
        for i in range(0, D, 4):
            for l in range(4):
                d = v[i+l]-q[i+l]
                s[l] += d*d
        out.append(sum(s))
    return out

for fn in (scalar, lane4):
    t = time.perf_counter(); r = fn(); dt = time.perf_counter()-t
    print('%-7s %d distances in %.3fs' % (fn.__name__, N, dt))
print('real kernels: AVX-512, 16 lanes, masked tails, CPUID dispatch')

title: GPU ANN at scale
description: GPUs scale ANN to billions: the index shards across GPU memory, queries stream through in batches, and throughput hits millions of QPS. cuVS (RAPIDS) provides GPU IVF-PQ and CAGRA (graph-based, GPU-native). The design constraints are GPU RAM (shard or compress to fit) and batch size (saturate the SMs). Single queries go to CPU; batches go to GPU.
mechanism: Shard index across GPUs; batch queries (1k+); GPU-native graph (CAGRA) or IVF-PQ kernels; results back over PCIe. Keep the hot index resident.
algo: Throughput scales with SMs; latency per batch ~constant to saturation. Index must fit GPU RAM.
demo:
# GPU ANN economics: when does the batch saturate the device?
SM, PER_SM_QPS = 128, 800  # streaming multiprocessors x per-SM throughput
MAX_QPS = SM * PER_SM_QPS

for batch in (1, 64, 1024, 16384):
    # toy model: fixed launch cost + per-query cost, capped by device max
    ms = 0.5 + batch * 0.002
    qps = min(batch / (ms/1000), MAX_QPS)
    print('batch %5d -> %.0f qps %s' % (batch, qps, '(saturated)' if qps >= MAX_QPS else ''))
print('single queries -> CPU; batches -> GPU; index must fit GPU RAM')

title: DiskANN: SSD-native search
description: DiskANN puts billion-vector graphs on SSD: the compressed graph stays in RAM, full vectors live on NVMe, and beam search fetches only the pages it visits (~100 SSD reads per query). It made billion-scale ANN affordable on one machine — no GPU farm. The graph is built for SSD access patterns (high degree, page-aligned), and queries re-rank with exact vectors fetched on demand.
mechanism: Build a high-degree graph (Vamana); store PQ codes in RAM, full vectors on SSD; beam search over codes, fetching full vectors for the final re-rank. ~3.5ms p99 on billion-scale.
algo: O(beam * degree) code comparisons + O(shortlist) SSD reads. IOPS, not RAM, is the budget.
demo:
# DiskANN pattern: RAM graph walk, SSD only for the re-rank shortlist
import random
random.seed(9)
N = 50000
codes = [random.randrange(256) for _ in range(N)]     # PQ codes in RAM
vectors = {i: random.gauss(0, 1) for i in range(N)}  # full precision on 'SSD'
reads = [0]

def ssd_get(i):
    reads[0] += 1
    return vectors[i]

qcode = 128
cands = sorted(range(N), key=lambda i: abs(codes[i]-qcode))[:200]  # RAM beam
best = min(cands, key=lambda i: abs(ssd_get(i)))                   # SSD re-rank
print('RAM scanned %d codes; SSD reads: %d (not %d)' % (N, reads[0], N))
print('billion-scale on one machine: the SSD is the memory hierarchy')

title: Filtered ANN search
description: Real queries filter AND search: 'red shoes, nearest to this image'. Filtered ANN pre-filters with the scalar index (bitmaps), then searches within the survivors — or searches first and filters after (better when the filter is unselective). The hard case is highly selective filters (few survivors): the graph walk starves. Modern engines handle it with filtered graph traversal (only visit matching nodes).
mechanism: Selective filter: bitmap -> candidate set -> exact/ANN within. Unselective: ANN first, filter after. Graph engines: traverse only nodes passing the filter (needs filter-aware graph or fallback).
algo: Cost = filter cost + ANN over survivors. Selective filters shrink the problem; unselective ones add overhead.
demo:
import random
random.seed(11)
N = 5000
colors = ['red' if random.random() < 0.05 else 'blue' for _ in range(N)]  # selective!
scores = [random.random() for _ in range(N)]

# plan A: filter first (bitmap), then top-k within survivors
survivors = [i for i in range(N) if colors[i] == 'red']
top_a = sorted(survivors, key=lambda i: -scores[i])[:5]
# plan B: top-k first, then filter (starves on selective filters)
top_b = [i for i in sorted(range(N), key=lambda i: -scores[i])[:50] if colors[i] == 'red'][:5]
print('selective filter (5%%): plan A finds %d, plan B finds %d' % (len(top_a), len(top_b)))
print('selective -> filter first; unselective -> search first, filter after')

title: Quantization-aware training
description: Post-training quantization loses recall because the embeddings were never optimized for it. Quantization-aware training adds the quantization to the training loop (or fine-tunes with a quantization penalty), so the model learns representations that survive compression. The gains are real — several recall points at the same bitrate — and it is why the best production vector stacks train with their deployment quantization in mind.
mechanism: Straight-through estimator for the quantization step during training; or contrastive fine-tuning with quantized negatives. Validate recall at the deployment bitrate, not at fp32.
algo: Training-time technique; inference unchanged. Recall gains of 2-5 points typical.
demo:
# quantization-aware idea: train with the noise you'll deploy with
import random
random.seed(13)

def quantize(x, bits=4):
    levels = 2 ** bits
    return round(x * levels) / levels

# 'embeddings' trained without awareness vs with simulated quantization noise
clean = [random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(100)]
# QAT: the model sees quantized values during training -> learns robust features
robust = [quantize(x + random.gauss(0, 0.05)) for x in clean]  # noise-augmented
plain_q = [quantize(x) for x in clean]

err_plain = sum(abs(a-b) for a, b in zip(clean, plain_q)) / len(clean)
print('plain post-training quantization error: %.4f' % err_plain)
print('QAT: train WITH quantization noise -> representations survive compression')
print('typical gain: 2-5 recall points at the same bitrate')

title: Range search
description: Range search finds all vectors within radius r of the query — not top-k, but 'everything close'. It matters for deduplication ('all near-duplicates'), geo queries, and threshold-based retrieval. Graph indexes handle it by expanding the beam until the frontier exceeds r; IVF scans lists until distances exceed r. The result size is unbounded, so production APIs page it.
mechanism: Beam search with radius cutoff instead of k cutoff; collect all within r. Deduplicate across IVF lists. Page results; cap with max_results for safety.
algo: O(results + search) — cost scales with answer size, unlike top-k.
demo:
import random, math
random.seed(15)
pts = [(random.gauss(0, 0), random.gauss(0, 0)) for _ in range(2000)]
q, r = (0.1, -0.1), 0.5

def dist(a, b):
    return math.dist(a, b)

within = [p for p in pts if dist(p, q) <= r]
print('range r=%.1f around %s: %d of %d points' % (r, q, len(within), len(pts)))
print('use: dedup (all near-duplicates), geo, threshold retrieval')
print('page the results: answer size is unbounded, unlike top-k')

title: Latency budgets for ANN
description: Sub-millisecond ANN is a budget, not a hope: the p99 must fit inside the request's total latency alongside everything else (network, business logic, rendering). Budgeting splits the milliseconds — 0.3ms for the ANN lookup inside a 50ms page render — and every component gets its slice. When the budget breaks, degrade gracefully: smaller efSearch, cached results, approximate fallback — never a timeout the user sees.
mechanism: Per-request deadline; ANN call gets its slice; on slice exhaustion return the best-so-far (beam search is interruptible). Track budget adherence per deployment; alert on drift.
algo: O(1) deadline checks; beam search's interruptibility is the graceful-degradation mechanism.
demo:
import time

BUDGET_MS = 0.8  # the ANN slice of a 50ms page render

def ann_search(deadline):
    checked, best = 0, None
    for i in range(100000):  # beam expansion (simulated)
        checked += 1
        if time.perf_counter() > deadline:
            return best, checked, 'deadline: returning best-so-far'
        best = i
    return best, checked, 'complete'

deadline = time.perf_counter() + BUDGET_MS / 1000
best, checked, status = ann_search(deadline)
print('budget %.1fms: checked %d candidates -> %s' % (BUDGET_MS, checked, status))
print('beam search is interruptible: degrade gracefully, never time out visibly')
